clue.text: King's is turned by informer

definitions.meaning: the surface offers something belonging to the King being spun round; the setter is quoting a courtroom phrase in which a witness turns what they know over to the prosecution
the one who does the turning is an accomplice who testifies against the rest of the gang, usually for a lighter sentence

explanation.surface: Something belonging to the King being turned round by a tell-tale.
explanation.walkthrough: To turn King's evidence is to testify against your own accomplices in return for leniency. The whole clue is that set phrase with its key word lifted out, and the apostrophe after 'King' is the only sign that anything is missing.
explanation.definitionFit: Evidence is what an informer turns: in the phrase King's evidence, the testimony an accomplice hands to the Crown.

clue.text: With which to get into a house, say on the house?

definitions.text: With which to get into a house, say
definitions.meaning: the surface offers somebody's home, the thing you need a key for; in the theatre the house is where the audience sits, and what gets you in is a ticket
the landlord's phrase for a drink nobody is charged for, so this house is a pub and the point of it is that nothing is paid

explanation.surface: Something that lets you into a house, with somebody else footing the bill.
explanation.walkthrough: The two houses are different buildings: the first is a theatre's auditorium, the second the pub whose landlord is buying. Neither is the house you live in, which is the one the sentence wants you to picture.
explanation.definitionFit: A free pass admits you to the house at a theatre, and costs nothing — which is what being on the house means.

clue.text: Sound at heart if at home

indicators.note: What lies at the heart of a phrase is buried in the middle of it, so the letters wanted are sitting inside these words already.

parts.note: six consecutive letters of this phrase, beginning one letter in

explanation.surface: Somebody who is sound at heart as long as they are in their own house.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sound' is the sailor's verb for measuring depth with a weighted line, not the noun the surface wants. A fathom is six feet of that line, still the unit on Admiralty charts.
explanation.definitionFit: To sound water is to measure how deep it is, and a fathom is the unit that measurement comes in — hence the verb to fathom.

clue.text: Scruffy type's flab spread with age

indicators.note: Flab that has spread has gone everywhere it was not before, and letters spread like that do not stay in the order they were printed in.

parts.note: four letters of fodder
three more, seven in all

explanation.surface: Middle-aged spread taking hold of somebody who was never tidy to begin with.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface is one unkind sentence about a waistline, and both of its nouns are raw material rather than description. A fleabag is British for anything squalid — a cheap hotel as readily as a person.
explanation.definitionFit: A fleabag is a dirty, unkempt person or place — literally one you would expect to be carrying fleas.

clue.text: See 2
Medic in ground with TNT charge

indicators.note: Anything ground has been through the mill and comes out in pieces that are no longer in the order they went in.

parts.note: seven letters of fodder, the little word pulled in with the doctor
the explosive's three letters join the shuffle, ten in all

explanation.surface: A doctor down in the earth with a stick of TNT alongside.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Charge' does double duty: TNT is measured out in charges and a court hands down the other kind, and only the legal sense is the definition. 'Ground' reads as the earth the medic is in.
explanation.definitionFit: An indictment is the formal written charge on which somebody is brought to trial.

clue.text: Food shop with cross on top of entrance, elevated and barred

indicators.note: The top of a word is the letter it starts with, and that single letter is all this asks for.
Something elevated has been lifted, and in a down entry lifting the letters makes them read from the bottom of the column upwards.

parts.note: a deli sells cold meats and cheese, which makes it a food shop
x = cross, the mark made on a ballot paper
the first letter of ENTRANCE

explanation.surface: A delicatessen with a cross above the door, up high, and shutters over the windows.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Barred' is the trap: it sounds like the bars on a shop front and means shut out of a country. Read the assembly from the bottom of the column and the whole thing turns over at once.
explanation.definitionFit: Somebody exiled has been barred from their own country, banishment being the strongest form of being shut out.

clue.text: Halve our shuttle service

indicators.note: A shuttle runs back and forth across a loom, and letters sent back and forth like that do not come to rest where they started.

parts.note: five letters of fodder
three more, eight in all

explanation.surface: A transport operator cutting the airport shuttle timetable in half.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Shuttle service' reads as one thing, the bus between terminals, and the setter needs it broken apart: the first word does the shuffling and the second is the definition. A car's service is an overhaul.
explanation.definitionFit: A service is the strip-down-and-check a garage gives a vehicle, which is what an overhaul is.

clue.text: Appropriate names acquired by a partner in the past

indicators.note: What has been acquired by somebody is now held by them, so these letters end up inside the pieces that did the acquiring.

parts.note: the article taken down as the single letter it is
a former husband, wife or partner is an ex
n = name, and the plural asks for it twice

explanation.surface: Names picked up from a former partner back in the day.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Appropriate' looks like the adjective meaning suitable and is the verb meaning to help yourself to something. To annex is to do that to territory, as a state does to a neighbour's province.
explanation.definitionFit: To annex land is to take it over as your own without being given it, which is what appropriating something is.

clue.text: Having no end to continental shelf is an advantage

indicators.note: A word having no end to it is a letter short at the finish, and that final letter is the one taken away here.

parts.note: a ledge is a shelf, whether on a wall or partway up a cliff
the letter standing at the end of CONTINENTAL, which is what goes

explanation.surface: The continental shelf running on with no end to it, which suits somebody.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Continental shelf' is a single geological thing in the surface and has to be split: one word supplies a letter to throw away and the other supplies the word to throw it out of. An edge over a rival is an advantage.
explanation.definitionFit: Having the edge on somebody is having the advantage over them, a margin in your favour rather than a physical rim.

clue.text: Side with health arrangement for capsule protection?

indicators.note: An arrangement of letters is whatever order somebody has put them in, which need not be the order they arrived in.

parts.note: four letters of fodder
six more, ten in all

explanation.surface: Backing a healthcare scheme that covers the packaging of pills.
explanation.walkthrough: The capsule is the spacecraft sort, not the pill, which is where the surface loses you. A heat shield is the layer on the underside of a re-entry capsule that burns away instead of the crew.
explanation.definitionFit: A returning space capsule meets air friction hot enough to destroy it, and the heat shield is the part that takes that instead — the capsule's protection.

clue.text: Accepted company is failing

parts.note: whatever is accepted is in — in favour, in fashion
a firm is a business company

explanation.surface: A business that has just been taken on is already going under.
explanation.walkthrough: Both halves read as one sentence about a struggling company, and 'is' is doing nothing but holding them together. Infirm is failing in the bodily sense, the word used of the old and frail.
explanation.definitionFit: Somebody infirm is failing in health and strength, which is the sense the word keeps in 'the aged and infirm'.

clue.text: Engrave 'swell' over end of the combine?

indicators.note: Here 'over' is covering rather than above: what is spread over a thing wraps round it, so the letter named goes inside the word laid over it.

parts.note: read as en-grave, in a grave: to inter a body is to put it in one

indicators.note: The end of a word is its final letter, and that single letter is all that is taken.

parts.note: a swell at sea is a long rolling wave
the final letter of THE, tucked in under the W

explanation.surface: Carving the word 'swell' onto the back end of a combine harvester.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Engrave' is not the instruction it looks like: split at the prefix it means to put in a grave, which is to inter. The combine of the surface is the harvester; the definition is the plain verb to combine.
explanation.definitionFit: To interweave strands is to combine them into one fabric, each thread ending up part of the others.

clue.text: Bent aide put off protecting territorial head

indicators.note: Something put off has been moved from where it was meant to be, and letters moved about like that come back in another order.
What protects a thing closes round it, so the shuffled letters go outside the one letter named next.

parts.note: seven letters of fodder

indicators.note: The head of a word is the letter at the front of it, and that one letter is all that is wanted.

parts.note: the first letter of TERRITORIAL, which the shuffled letters close around

explanation.surface: A crooked assistant, told to wait, shielding the local boss.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bent' reads as the adjective for a crooked aide and is the noun the answer needs. A bent for languages is an inclination you were born with, the same picture as a leaning.
explanation.definitionFit: A bent for something is a natural talent for it, which is exactly what an aptitude is.

clue.text: What can cause a failure to appreciate music? An organ can at first

indicators.note: The piece told to come at first is the one written down before the other, whichever order the clue happens to name them in.

parts.note: a can of beans is also named after the metal it is plated with
one of the organs of the body, and the one that does the listening

explanation.surface: Asking what deafens somebody to music, then offering a church organ.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Can' turns up twice, once as the ordinary verb of the question and once as the thing on the kitchen shelf. The two pieces have to be written down in the reverse of the order the clue gives them.
explanation.definitionFit: Somebody with a tin ear cannot hear the difference between one note and the next, so music is wasted on them.

clue.text: Get through Don's confiscated article

indicators.note: What has been confiscated has been taken and kept, so the piece seized ends up held inside the word that took it.

parts.note: to don a coat is to wear it
the definite article, taken as its three letters

explanation.surface: A university don who has had somebody's newspaper piece taken off him.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Don' looks like the Oxford teacher and is the verb for putting clothes on. To weather a storm is to come through it still afloat, which is where the definition's 'through' comes from.
explanation.definitionFit: To weather a crisis is to get through it and survive, the metaphor being a ship that rides out the storm.

clue.text: See 15
Dishevelled, drunk, empty? Dry out!

indicators.note: Letters told to come out are taken away from the string they were part of, leaving the rest standing.

parts.note: the two words run together into one string of ten letters
the three letters of DRY are what leave: the D and R that open the string and the Y that closes it

explanation.surface: A drunk with an empty glass being ordered to sober up.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Dry out!' reads as advice to the drunk and is the instruction to lose three letters. Nothing is shuffled afterwards — what is left already stands in the right order. Kempt is the old past participle of comb, so unkempt hair is uncombed.
explanation.definitionFit: Unkempt means uncombed and untidy, which of a person or their hair is dishevelled.

clue.text: Is lip/gum hurt by this activity?

definitions.text: Is lip/gum hurt by this activity?

indicators.note: Something hurt has been knocked about, and letters knocked about come out in an order they did not go in.

parts.note: eight letters of fodder, the slash being punctuation rather than instruction

explanation.surface: A question about whether lips and gums come off badly in some unnamed pastime.
explanation.walkthrough: Every word does both jobs at once: the first three spell the sport, and boxing really is the activity that leaves lips and gums damaged. Pugilism is from Latin pugil, a boxer.
explanation.definitionFit: Pugilism is the formal name for boxing, and the whole clue reads straight as a question about what boxing does to a mouth.

clue.text: Piano makes you elated — just

parts.note: somebody in high spirits is up
a just decision is the right one

explanation.surface: A piano that lifts your mood, and only barely.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Just' at the end reads as 'barely', finishing the joke about mild elation; the sense wanted is the one in 'a just cause'. An upright is the piano with vertical strings that stands against a wall.
explanation.definitionFit: An upright is the household piano, built with its strings vertical so it fits flat against a wall rather than lying open like a grand.

clue.text: Musical stagehand's lock retainer

parts.note: the hippie-era rock musical, on Broadway in 1968 and revived ever since
a grip is the crew member who shifts the scenery and the gear

explanation.surface: Somebody working backstage on a musical, in charge of a lock.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Lock' means a curl of hair here, not the fitting on a door, and both pieces of the wordplay come out of the theatre. A hairgrip is what Americans call a bobby pin.
explanation.definitionFit: A hairgrip is the sprung metal pin — a kirby grip — that holds a lock of hair in place.

clue.text: Agreement to link air conditioning with cable

parts.note: ac is the everyday short form for air conditioning
a cord is a length of flexible cable

explanation.surface: Wiring an air-conditioning unit up to a cable.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface is an electrician's afternoon and 'to link' does nothing but join the halves — the app greys such words out because beginners hunt for wordplay in them. An accord is the word used for agreements between states, as in the Helsinki Accords.
explanation.definitionFit: An accord is an agreement, the term reached for when the parties are governments or sides in a dispute.

clue.text: Power failure abroad goes on a long time

parts.note: somebody out of the country is abroad
waiting an age is waiting a long time

explanation.surface: A blackout in some other country dragging on and on.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is the first two words and the rest of the sentence reads as though it were still describing them, which is why 'abroad' looks like scene-setting rather than a piece to spell out. An age, informally, is any wait that feels endless.
explanation.definitionFit: An outage is the stretch of time when the supply is out, the standard word for a power cut.

clue.text: Get boat moving with current

indicators.note: A boat that is moving is no longer where it was, and letters that move about will not stay in the order given.

parts.note: four letters of fodder
whatever is current is in — in vogue, in fashion

explanation.surface: Getting a boat under way with the help of the current.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Current' looks like the flow of water carrying the boat along and is the fashion sense instead. Only the four letters of the boat are shuffled; the other two join on at the end as they stand.
explanation.definitionFit: To obtain something is to get it, the formal verb sitting where the plain one would do.

clue.text: Diagram maker matches its bends

indicators.note: Letters that bend are pulled out of the straight line they came in, so they do not stay in their printed order.

parts.note: seven letters of fodder
three more, ten in all

explanation.surface: Somebody drawing a plan that follows every curve of the thing in front of them.
explanation.walkthrough: Read straight the sentence says the drawing keeps up with its subject, so the last word looks like part of that picture. A schematist is one who draws up schemes — the -ist noun behind 'schematic'.
explanation.definitionFit: A schematist draws up schemes and schematics, so the word names the person who makes the diagram rather than the diagram itself.

clue.text: To collapse after fellow's gone is not common

indicators.note: What has gone is no longer there, so the letter named just before it comes out of the word it was in.

parts.note: to faint is to collapse in a heap
f = fellow, as in Fellow of the Royal Society
no letters from this one: it is the setter's register label, marking the answer as vulgar speech rather than standard English

explanation.surface: Somebody keeling over once the fellow has left, which is nothing unusual.
explanation.walkthrough: The last word is not part of the definition: it marks the register, telling you the two words wanted are run together the way the grammar books disapprove of. 'Fellow' is the F of FRS.
explanation.definitionFit: Ain't is the contraction that stands in for 'is not' — and for am not and are not — in speech that no style guide will have.

clue.text: Lawyer — southern kind

parts.note: s = southern, as on a compass or a signpost
people of that ilk are people of that kind

explanation.surface: A barrister from the south of a particular sort.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Kind' is the noun, not the adjective for a nice lawyer. A silk is a King's or Queen's Counsel, so called because reaching that rank brings the right to a silk gown instead of a stuff one.
explanation.definitionFit: A silk is a senior British barrister, a KC or QC, named for the silk gown the rank entitles them to wear in court.

clue.text: Fish is brought up by line at depth

indicators.note: In a down entry what is brought up is read from the bottom of the column towards the top, so these two letters change places.

parts.note: the two letters of IS, hauled up the column the other way round
l = line, as on a map or a railway timetable
d = depth, the third dimension after length and width

explanation.surface: A fish hauled up on a line from deep water.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Is' is not joinery here: it is two letters of the answer, turned round. A sild is a young herring, the Norwegian word, and it reaches Britain in tins.
explanation.definitionFit: A sild is a small young herring, the Scandinavian fish sold tinned in oil or tomato sauce.

clue.text: Forced to dispose of top cut

indicators.note: To dispose of something is to get rid of it, and the top of a word is the letter it begins with, so that first letter goes.

parts.note: a driven person is forced along, by circumstance or by somebody else

explanation.surface: Being made to throw away the prime cut of meat.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Top cut' reads as the butcher's best joint and has to come apart, one word giving an instruction and the other the definition. Riven means split — a tree riven by lightning, a party riven by argument.
explanation.definitionFit: Something riven has been torn or split apart, which is to say cut in two.

clue.text: Husband: stuffy, with nothing up top

definitions.note: The answer is an adjective and the definition a noun phrase, but 'nothing up top' is only ever used of a person — he has nothing up top — so it substitutes in the same slot.

parts.note: h = husband, the abbreviation from family trees and census forms
a stuffy room is one with no air moving in it

explanation.surface: A dull, stuffy husband with not much going on upstairs.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Nothing up top' is the idiom for being thick, and the setter means it literally: no hair on the head. The colon does nothing but let the surface read as a character sketch.
explanation.definitionFit: Somebody hairless has nothing on top of their head, which is the literal reading of a phrase that usually calls a person stupid.
